newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. May PPI falls 0.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. May PPI falls 0.3 pct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported the Producer Price Index (PPI) fell 0.3 percent in May.
Minus food and energy items, the core PPI was off 0.3 percent. In April, PPI dropped 0.6 percent, while the core down 0.1 percent.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a 0.1 percent rise both overall and in the core.
VINCENT MALANGA, PRESIDENT, LASALLE ECONOMICS,: "I think this was a great report, and (the trend) is likely to continue.
"Over the next three months, we're probably more likely to see continued negative numbers on the PPI, and perhaps even the CPI, than positive numbers.
"The PPI showed a decline in car prices; that's likely continuing as well."

ASTRID ADOLFSON, VICE PRESIDENT AND SENIOR ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "The auto sector was a main reason (for the decline). It basically shows that there is no inflation in the manufacturing sector.
"I don't think the (Federal Reserve) has any reason to move; the only thing I would suggest is we wait for the core Consumer Price Index to make sure that it is true."

HUGH JOHNSON, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, FIRST ALBANY CORP: "It's just remarkable. There's no question that there's very little sign of upward pressure on prices at the wholesale level; there's no sign of significant upward pressure at the consumer level, so inflation remains surprisingly very benign.
"At this very, very late stage in a business recovery -- over six years -- to have inflation this benign is remarkable.
"I think part of the explanation is the changing structure of the economy ... downward prices on energy prices this year helps explain it, the very strong dollar helps explain it.
"The dollar is more important now because of the internationalization of the economy and I think maybe those factors are underappreciated."

SAM KAHAN, PRESIDENT, ASK FINANCIAL RESEARCH LTD: "Despite the economy working barely at high levels of output and despite the tight labor markets, these have yet to be translated into increasing prices."
He said that along with a weak retail sales report on Thursday, "it makes it less likely the Fed will do anything at its July meeting."

JOSEPH DZIWURA, VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, SAKURA BANK LTD: "No Fed move on the horizon. The only thing I can say is that the crude (goods) core was up 1.2 percent. That's the only troubling part of the report. Everything else is fairly subdued.
"The Fed isn't out of the picture this year completely. We think the Fed is likely to have one more move this year. There is some pipeline (inflation) pressure to be concerned about."
DAVID JONES, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AUBREY G. LANSTON & CO: "It's better news than expected. The consensus was for a modest increase and the report turned out to be even more favorable.

"Those five consecutive monthly declines in producer prices suggesting certainly that in the goods producing sector, there's not the slightest hint of a pick-up in price pressures despite full employment conditions in the economy.
"It's a situation that's almost too good to be true but I think both the bond and the stock markets will enjoy the situation anyway.

"Bonds have already dropped after the subdued retail sales report yesterday. Now the second shoe drops with amazingly good price statistics. At least in terms of the financial markets, it just doesn't get any better than this.
"I do think this sets the stage for a rebound in the third and fourth quarters as consumers see gains in financial asset prices and job and income pushes confidence higher.
"Price pressures are non-existent particularly in the goods producing sector. Consumer prices next week will likely be favorable as well.

"There are some hints of higher prices in travel, hotels, transportation. But even there I see only modest, at most, upward pressure on prices. Prices at the intermediate stage of production are very well behaved.

"We did get a rebound in crude core inflation -- up 1.2 percent after a 2.3 percent decline in the April numbers. That was based on prices of industrial raw materials going up -- metals and other raw materials.
"It's possible that as the year wears on we might see some increased pressure in the pipeline. But for now it's a remarkably good inflation performance and financial markets like that.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
